extracted.intended_audience: practitioners before the USPTO (registered patent attorneys and patent agents), applicants for registration/recognition, and law firms/practitioners providing patent-related services
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and rules governing ethical conduct, conflicts, communications, fees, confidentiality, advertising, discipline, and practitioner duties for persons practicing before the United States Patent and Trademark Office (USPTO). Primarily addresses registered patent practitioners (attorneys and agents).

rubrics_metrics.name: Belief or believes (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: “Belief” or “believes” denotes that the person involved actually supposed the fact in question to be true. A person’s belief may be inferred from circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definition used to interpret obligations where the Rules refer to a practitioner’s 'belief' or what a practitioner 'believes'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confirmed in writing (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: “Confirmed in writing,” when used in reference to the informed consent of a person, denotes informed consent that is given in writing by the person or a writing that a lawyer/practitioner promptly transmits to the person confirming an oral informed consent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If infeasible to obtain or transmit the writing at the time of consent, the practitioner must obtain or transmit it within a reasonable time thereafter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Firm or law firm (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: “Firm” or “law firm” denotes a lawyer/practitioner or lawyers/practitioners in a law partnership, professional corporation, sole proprietorship or other association authorized to practice law; or lawyers/practitioners employed in a legal services organization or the legal department of a corporation or other organization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to determine when rules that apply to firms impose obligations across associated practitioners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fraud or fraudulent (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: “Fraud” or “fraudulent” denotes conduct that involves a misrepresentation of material fact made with intent to deceive or a state of mind so reckless respecting consequences as to be the equivalent of intent, where there is justifiable reliance and resulting injury; may include purposeful omission that makes other statements misleading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definition added to interpret misconduct provisions and disclosure exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Informed consent (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: “Informed consent” denotes the agreement by a person to a proposed course of conduct after the practitioner has communicated adequate information and explanation about the material risks of and reasonably available alternatives to the proposed course of conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key standard for many consent-based exceptions and waivers (e.g., limiting scope, conflicts, third-party payments).

rubrics_metrics.name: Knowingly, known, or knows (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: “Knowingly,” “known,” or “knows” denotes actual knowledge of the fact in question. A person’s knowledge may be inferred from circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to evaluate scienter-based obligations and prohibitions (e.g., knowingly making false statements).

rubrics_metrics.name: Partner (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: “Partner” denotes a member of a partnership, a shareholder in a law firm organized as a professional corporation, or a member of an association authorized to practice law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Terminology for applying firm-imputation rules and firm identity rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law-related services (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Law-related services means services that might reasonably be performed in conjunction with and in substance are related to the provision of legal services, and that are not prohibited as unauthorized practice of law when provided by a non-lawyer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guides what non-lawyer-provided services may nonetheless be regulated/connected to practitioner duties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Person (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Person means an individual, a corporation, an association, a trust, a partnership, and any other organization or legal entity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defines who can be a client or subject to duties under the Rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable or reasonably (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reasonable or reasonably when used in relation to conduct by a practitioner means the conduct of a reasonably prudent and competent practitioner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard of care reference for duties like diligence, communication, and screening.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable belief or reasonably believes (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reasonable belief or reasonably believes when used in reference to a practitioner means that the practitioner believes the matter in question and that the circumstances are such that the belief is reasonable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to assess when a practitioner's belief justifies action or exception (e.g., conflicts consent).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonably should know (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reasonably should know when used in reference to a practitioner means that a practitioner of reasonable prudence and competence would ascertain the matter in question.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Imposes an objective inquiry obligation on practitioners to investigate facts they reasonably should have known.

rubrics_metrics.name: Screened (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Screened means the isolation of a practitioner from any participation in a matter through the timely imposition of procedures within a firm that are reasonably adequate under the circumstances to protect information that the isolated practitioner is obligated to protect under these Rules or other law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defines what constitutes effective screening for conflict-imputation exceptions; guidance emphasizes timeliness and adequacy of procedures and protection of confidential information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substantial (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Substantial when used in reference to degree or extent denotes a material matter of clear and weighty importance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to determine when an interest, injury, or fact rises to the level that triggers or justifies duties/exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tribunal (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tribunal denotes a court, an arbitrator in a binding arbitration proceeding or a legislative body, administrative agency or other body acting in an adjudicative capacity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarifies scope of rules that refer to proceedings before a 'tribunal' (includes the USPTO Office when acting adjudicatively).

rubrics_metrics.name: Writing or written (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Writing or written means a tangible or electronic record of a communication or representation, including handwriting, typewriting, printing, photostating, photography, audio or video recording and electronic communications. A 'signed' writing includes an electronic sound, symbol or process attached to or logically associated with a writing and executed or adopted by a person with the intent to sign the writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Broad definition includes electronic signatures and records for required confirmations and fee agreements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 1.1 Competence
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall provide competent representation to a client. Competent representation requires the legal, scientific, and technical knowledge, skill, thoroughness and preparation reasonably necessary for the representation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Competence extends beyond legal knowledge to include scientific and technical knowledge for patent practice; lack of these elements can violate the rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 1.2 Scope of Representation & Allocation of Authority
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall abide by a client’s decisions concerning the objectives of representation and, as required by communication rules, shall consult with the client as to the means by which they are to be pursued. A practitioner may limit the scope of representation if reasonable and with the client’s informed consent. A practitioner shall not counsel or assist a client to engage in conduct the practitioner knows is criminal or fraudulent but may discuss legal consequences and make good-faith efforts to determine the law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes special application to settlements, criminal pleas (where applicable), and the requirement that scope limitations be reasonable and informed-consent based.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 1.3 Diligence
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall act with reasonable diligence and promptness in representing a client.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Obligation applies to timely prosecution of applications, meeting deadlines, responding to clients and avoiding neglect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 1.4 Communication
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall: (1) promptly inform the client of any decision or circumstance requiring the client’s informed consent; (2) reasonably consult with the client about the means to accomplish objectives; (3) keep the client reasonably informed about the status of the matter; (4) promptly comply with reasonable requests for information; and (5) consult with the client about any limitation on the practitioner’s conduct when client expects assistance not permitted by the Rules. A practitioner shall explain a matter to the extent reasonably necessary to permit the client to make informed decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasizes prompt notices (e.g., decisions requiring consent), regular status updates, responsive information sharing and clear explanations to enable client decision-making.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 1.5 Fees (reasonableness and disclosure)
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall not make an agreement for, charge, or collect an unreasonable fee or an unreasonable amount for expenses. Factors to determine reasonableness include time and labor, novelty and difficulty, skill required, likelihood of precluding other employment, customary local fee, amount involved and results obtained, time limitations, nature and length of professional relationship, experience/reputation/ability of practitioner, and whether fee is fixed or contingent. The scope and basis/rate of fee and expenses should be communicated to the client, preferably in writing, before or within a reasonable time after commencing representation. Contingent fees must be in writing and set out method of calculation and expenses; upon conclusion the practitioner must provide an accounting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also covers division of fees between practitioners (must be proportional to services or joint responsibility, client agreement confirmed in writing, total fee reasonable), and identifies matters where contingent fees are prohibited or conditions where fee divisions are permitted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 1.6 Confidentiality of Information
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall not reveal information relating to the representation of a client unless the client gives informed consent, disclosure is impliedly authorized to carry out the representation, or the disclosure is permitted by specified exceptions. A practitioner may reveal information to the extent reasonably necessary to: (1) prevent reasonably certain death or substantial bodily harm; (2) prevent the client from committing a crime/fraud reasonably certain to result in substantial injury to another and in furtherance of which client used practitioner’s services; (3) prevent, mitigate or rectify substantial injury to another caused by client’s crime/fraud or inequitable conduct before the Office; (4) secure legal advice about compliance with the Rules; (5) establish a claim or defense on behalf of the practitioner in a controversy with the client or respond to allegations concerning the practitioner’s representation; or (6) comply with law or court order. A practitioner shall disclose to the Office information necessary to comply with applicable duty of disclosure provisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balances client confidentiality with narrow exceptions for preventing serious harm, fraud/inequitable conduct (including before the Office), compliance advice, self-defense, and legal compulsion; includes specific duty-to-Office disclosure in patent prosecution contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 1.7 Conflict of Interest: Current Clients
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall not represent a client if the representation involves a concurrent conflict of interest, which exists if (1) representation of one client will be directly adverse to another, or (2) there is a significant risk that representation will be materially limited by responsibilities to another client, former client, third person, or by a personal interest. Notwithstanding this, representation is permitted if the practitioner reasonably believes they can provide competent/diligent representation to each affected client; the representation is not prohibited by law; it does not involve asserting claims by one client against another in the same litigation or proceeding before a tribunal; and each affected client gives informed consent, confirmed in writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requires objective assessment of significant risk of material limitation and written informed consent when waiving conflicts; prohibits certain adverse-claim scenarios even with consent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 1.8 Conflict of Interest: Specific Rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific prohibitions and requirements when practitioners interact with clients in transactional contexts: (a) business transactions with clients or acquiring adverse pecuniary interests require fairness, full written disclosure, advising client in writing of seeking independent counsel, and client’s informed written consent; (b) cannot use information relating to representation to client’s disadvantage without informed consent except as permitted; (c) cannot solicit substantial gifts from clients except to related persons; (d) cannot make literary or media-rights agreements prior to conclusion of representation; (e) limitations on providing financial assistance to clients with exceptions (advancing costs, representing indigent clients, advancing costs for Office proceedings with client ultimately liable, advancing fees to prevent abandonment due to practitioner error); (f) accepting compensation from third parties requires client informed consent, no interference with independence, and protection of client information; (g) aggregate settlements require each client’s informed written consent and disclosure of claims/participation; (h)-(k) other prohibitions apply (e.g., prospective limitation of malpractice liability requires independent representation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detailed requirements protect clients from unfair transactions, preserve independence of judgment, regulate financial assistance and fee arrangements, and require written informed consents and disclosures in many contexts; includes patent-specific allowances (e.g., taking interest in patent/application as part of fee).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 1.9 Duties to Former Clients
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner who formerly represented a client shall not thereafter represent another person in the same or a substantially related matter in which that person’s interests are materially adverse to the former client unless the former client gives informed consent, confirmed in writing. A practitioner shall not knowingly represent a person in such a matter where the former firm represented the client and the practitioner acquired information protected by confidentiality that is material to the matter unless former client consents. A practitioner shall not use or reveal information relating to former representation to that former client’s disadvantage except as permitted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Protects former clients’ confidences and prevents adverse use of material information acquired previously; consent must be informed and written where required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 1.10 Imputation of Conflicts of Interest
rubrics_metrics.description: While practitioners are associated in a firm, none shall knowingly represent a client when any one of them practicing alone would be prohibited from doing so by conflict rules, unless: (1) the prohibition is based on a personal interest of the disqualified practitioner and does not present a significant risk to remaining practitioners' representation; or (2) the prohibition is based upon prior firm association and the disqualified practitioner is timely screened from participation, apportioned no part of the fee, and written notice is given to any affected former client describing the screening procedures and compliance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allows screening and notice to avoid imputation when appropriate; emphasizes apportionment of fees and prompt notice to former clients as conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 7.3 Direct Contact With Prospective Clients
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall not by in-person, live telephone or real-time electronic contact solicit professional employment from a prospective client when a significant motive is pecuniary gain, unless the person contacted is a practitioner or has a family, close personal, or prior professional relationship with the practitioner. A practitioner shall not solicit by written, recorded or electronic communication or by in-person, telephone or real-time contact if the prospective client has made known a desire not to be solicited or if the solicitation involves coercion, duress or harassment. Written/recorded/electronic communications soliciting professional employment from a prospective client known to need legal services in a particular matter must include the words “Advertising Material” on the outside envelope and at the beginning and ending of any recorded/electronic communication (unless recipient is a practitioner or has a specified relationship). Participation in prepaid or group legal service plans that use in-person or telephone contact is allowed under specified conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Restricts direct solicitation to protect vulnerable prospective clients; requires clear labeling of advertising and allows limited exceptions for practitioner-to-practitioner or close-relationship contacts and specified plans.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 7.4 Communication of Fields of Practice and Specialization
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner may communicate the fact that they do or do not practice in particular fields of law. Registered practitioners who are attorneys may use designations like 'Patents', 'Patent Attorney', 'Registered Patent Attorney' or similar; non-attorney registered patent agents may use 'Patents', 'Patent Agent', 'Registered Patent Agent' or similar. A practitioner shall not state or imply certification as a specialist unless certified by an organization approved by an appropriate state authority or accredited by the American Bar Association and the name of the certifying organization is clearly identified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permits truthful practice-area statements and specific patent-related titles for registered practitioners, while protecting against misleading claims of specialization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 7.5 Firm Names and Letterheads
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall not use a firm name, letterhead or other professional designation that violates rules on communications about services. A trade name may be used if it does not imply a connection with a government agency or public/charitable legal services organization and is not otherwise misleading. A law firm with offices in more than one jurisdiction may use the same name in each jurisdiction, but identification of lawyers in an office must indicate jurisdictional limitations for those not licensed where the office is located. The name of a practitioner holding public office shall not be used in the name of a law firm during any substantial period when the practitioner is not actively and regularly practicing with the firm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requires truthful firm identification and accurate representation of lawyers' jurisdictional authority and current practice status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 8.1 Registration, Recognition and Disciplinary Matters
rubrics_metrics.description: An applicant for registration/recognition or a practitioner in connection with registration, recognition, disciplinary or reinstatement matters shall not knowingly make a false statement of material fact, fail to disclose a fact necessary to correct a misapprehension known to have arisen, fail to cooperate with the Office of Enrollment and Discipline, or knowingly fail to respond to a lawful demand or request for information, except where information is protected by confidentiality rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Imposes honesty and cooperation obligations in admissions/disciplinary contexts; confidentiality exceptions still apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 8.2 Judicial and Legal Officials
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall not make a statement that the practitioner knows to be false or with reckless disregard as to its truth or falsity concerning the qualifications or integrity of a judge, adjudicatory officer or public legal officer, or of a candidate for such office. A practitioner who is a candidate for judicial office shall comply with the applicable Code of Judicial Conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Protects reputation and integrity of adjudicative officers and requires candidate practitioners to follow judicial conduct rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 8.3 Reporting Professional Misconduct
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner who knows that another practitioner has committed a violation of the USPTO Rules of Professional Conduct raising a substantial question as to that practitioner’s honesty, trustworthiness or fitness as a practitioner shall inform the OED Director and any other appropriate professional authority. A practitioner who knows that a judge, hearing officer, administrative patent/trademark judge, or similar official has committed a violation raising a substantial question as to fitness shall inform the appropriate authority. This requirement does not compel disclosure of information protected by confidentiality rules or information gained while participating in an approved lawyers assistance program.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Creates a duty to report serious ethical breaches while preserving confidentiality exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 8.4 Misconduct
rubrics_metrics.description: It is professional misconduct for a practitioner to: (a) violate or attempt to violate the USPTO Rules of Professional Conduct or knowingly assist/induce another to do so; (b) commit a criminal act that reflects adversely on honesty, trustworthiness or fitness; (c) engage in dishonesty, fraud, deceit or misrepresentation; (d) engage in conduct prejudicial to the administration of justice; (e) state or imply an ability to improperly influence a government agency or official or to achieve results by means that violate the Rules or law; (f) knowingly assist a judge or judicial officer in conduct violating rules or law; (g) knowingly assist an officer or employee of the Office in conduct violating rules or law; (h) be publicly disciplined on ethical/professional misconduct grounds by a duly constituted authority; or (i) engage in other conduct that adversely reflects on fitness to practice before the Office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Broadly enumerates types of misconduct that can trigger discipline, including conviction, fraud, deceit, improper influence claims, assisting officials to violate rules, public discipline elsewhere, and other adverse conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 8.5 Disciplinary Authority; Choice of Law
rubrics_metrics.description: Disciplinary Authority: A practitioner admitted to practice in a jurisdiction is subject to that jurisdiction’s disciplinary authority regardless of where the conduct occurs. A practitioner not admitted in a jurisdiction is subject to disciplinary authority there if the practitioner provides or offers to provide any legal services in that jurisdiction. Choice of Law: For conduct in connection with a matter pending before a tribunal, the rules of the jurisdiction in which the tribunal sits apply (unless tribunal rules provide otherwise); for other conduct, the rules of the jurisdiction in which the practitioner’s conduct occurred apply, or if the predominant effect of the conduct is in a different jurisdiction, the rules of that jurisdiction apply. A practitioner is not subject to discipline if the conduct conforms to rules of a jurisdiction in which the practitioner reasonably believes the predominant effect will occur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains how multiple jurisdictions' rules may be applied in disciplinary proceedings and when a practitioner may avoid discipline by reasonable reliance on another jurisdiction’s rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: § 11.901 Savings clause
rubrics_metrics.description: A disciplinary proceeding based on conduct engaged in prior to the effective date of these regulations may be instituted subsequently if such conduct would continue to justify disciplinary sanctions under these regulations. No practitioner shall be subject to disciplinary proceeding under this part based on pre-effective-date conduct if such conduct would not have been subject to disciplinary action before such effective date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides transitional protection/clarity regarding retroactivity of the Rules.
